prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms enabled frequency standards with fractional uncertainty at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. I opened with the cavity method (B025) and moved because the scientific case for B057 survived every objection I could raise, not because of the count of supporters. The idea is one concrete, bounded concept, a magic-wavelength lattice that cancels light shifts while thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated in parallel, and it produced a measured result, fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, that independent national laboratories reproduce and routinely compare. It changes what can be asked of nature in the laboratory: constancy of fundamental constants, gravitational redshift over millimetre to metre scales, and relativistic geodesy. The credit is compact: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking strontium lattice clocks to record accuracy and stability and for the many-body and comparison work. In answer to the chair's questions, I think the citation can and should name the lattice and the magic wavelength explicitly, which separates it from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems. I regard the pending redefinition of the second as irrelevant to timing: it is a metrological decision that follows from a completed scientific result, and I have dropped my earlier suggestion that recognition might be slightly early.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a real reservation and not only a drafting problem. A sceptic can still read the lattice clock as the best refinement of a precision-measurement tradition and not as a new phenomenon, and I cannot fully answer that on the facts alone; it rests on whether one counts a new architecture with a new error budget as an invention in the sense of the will. The two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups, and the earlier trapping ideas of Ido and Kimble. I accept that the concept credit is not completely isolated, and I would not want the citation to claim more than the 1e-18 realisation and the magic-wavelength demonstration. My abandoned first choice, the cavity method, is arguably deeper as an idea but is not a single discovery with a clean attribution or a clean separation from the 2021 prize, and it is not mature as a matter of experiment, so I do not advance it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (B053) for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a mature theory-plus-experiment trio, and accepts B057 as a good outcome, with the disagreement being about framing and weight.
responses.response: I ranked B053 third and still treat it as a serious alternative, so I do not dispute worthiness. My difficulty is exactly the one you list: the Z2 classification and the HgTe experiment are a coherent core, but Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan sit outside three names, and the 2016 prize on topological phases means the committee has to say what is new beyond it. For B057 the attribution is cleaner and the experimental outcome is a number that can be checked, so I would not move B053 ahead. If B057 were set aside, I would support Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the core, with the Hasan versus Mele question unresolved in my mind.

responses.point: Kroll argues that magic-wavelength trapping opens a new regime of measurement, that the scientific achievement is complete without the redefinition of the second, and that he does not think a third name is needed. He also discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree on the timing: the redefinition is a consequence, not a condition, and I have changed my own view on that after your argument. On the Hall connection, a stay in the laboratory of a laureate whose frequency-comb work is a technical ingredient is a disciplinary closeness, not a tie to Katori or Ye, and I would not ask for recusal on the documented facts. It is for the chair to judge, and I would only ask that it be recorded. I also hold to my round-1 point on B005: five names for three places is not resolved, so it does not compete with the clock this year.

responses.point: Olsson accepts B057 as surviving every test, but treats the frequency-comb and single-ion overlap as a real reservation and asks whether the citation should explicitly separate the lattice clock from single-ion clocks and the 2005 work.
responses.response: I agree that the citation must do the separating work. My wording is that the invention is the optical lattice clock, with magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and that the stability comes from parallel interrogation of many atoms. That sentence is true of neither combs nor single-ion clocks. I do not think the reservation is fatal, but I take your point that it is a genuine one: the committee should not pretend the overlap is absent, only that it is bounded.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube (B054) to B057 as the stronger case, while still regarding IceCube as a major achievement whose source-level associations remain of modest significance, and asks whether the pending redefinition and the other lattice groups matter.
responses.response: I think your move is right on the merits. A new observational window is a strong argument, but the flux is secure and the source identifications are few, and the credit for three people against AMANDA, Baikal, DUMAND and a very large collaboration is not something I can defend in a citation today. I would regard IceCube as a candidate for a later year, not this one. On the other lattice groups, I would not let them block a two-name prize: that limit applies to most candidates on this list.

responses.point: Danielsson considers lattice clocks timely but not urgent, would separate them from earlier comb and ion-clock recognition, and does not think the pending redefinition should make the committee rush.
responses.response: I agree that there should be no rush, but I would go further: I do not think the redefinition should enter the deliberation at all, in either direction. If the committee waits for it, it is waiting for an administrative event, not for further science. Your point that the discovery side, tests of constancy of nature, is what makes this a physics prize is the argument I would put in the citation context.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that a new clock architecture with magic-wavelength trapping is a sufficiently distinct invention from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes.

Whether two names are enough given Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Takamoto, the ion-clock groups and the earlier Ido and Kimble trapping ideas, which I judge not to justify a third name but cannot prove from memory.
Whether B053 would be better supported if the credit among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang could be settled and the overlap with the 2016 prize explained.
My recollection of some technical details of the lattice-clock comparisons and of the cavity-method literature is from memory and has not been checked against sources.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or any other candidate, and I have no recusal to declare. My field of statistical physics of complex systems is close to the cavity-method candidate B025, which I no longer prefer, so that proximity does not touch my preferred configuration. I note the Hall connection disclosed by Kroll and leave its handling to the chair.
